Tori Trades · the bounce, trade by trade: its best and worst trades, and when it pays

This notebook replays one fixed line setting of her trendline bounce over a stock's whole 1-minute history, long and short, starting with NOW. It logs every trade with its trendlines. Each side is replayed alone: long only, then short only. In one shared wallet, a short holding the money would hide a long trade, and the other way round. Part 1 · the trades
  • §1 The trade log. Every long and every short trade, ranked by its return after costs and split into fifths. Each row has the line the trade bounced off and how many upward and downward lines stood when it was set up. The best five of each side are picked; click rows to pick others.
  • §2 The picked trades, each in its own chart. The 15-minute candles from a few sessions before the entry to a few after the exit. Every line that stood at the setup is drawn, upward and downward, with its anchors. The chart also shows the entry gap, the entry, the stop at every close and the exit, and the trade is told in words.
Part 2 · when does it pay?
  • §3–§5 Profitable time ranges. A zigzag cuts each side's record into rising and falling legs. A rising leg of a few trades is a profitable range. The ranges are labelled in hindsight: they are what a regime metric would have to predict.
  • §6 Luck. Do the wins cluster more than random deals of the same trades would?

data.text/html: The line setting: #417 without its trend filter. tune.py v2, TPE on the lower bound, trial 417: the one setting that held from Jan-Jul to Aug-Sep 2026 on a real sample (nine other stocks, t 2.3 then 2.1 against random holds, +10.6 then +9.0 bp a trade), and lost in 2025 (-7.7 bp). Its 400-session trend filter is off here: a trend filter is itself a regime metric, one of the candidates this study should test, not build into its labels (on NOW it leaves the longs no trade after November 2025). Without a trend filter the random trials did no worse (best median t of every trend value, in both windows). Distances are in typical candles (the stock's median 15-minute range at the time), so a value means the same on a calm and on a jumpy stock.

1 · The trade log

Every trade of each side, ranked by its return after costs. profit fifth splits a side's trades into five equal groups, 1 the most profitable fifth and 5 the least. Each row has the line the trade bounced off: the chart it was drawn on and its points A and B. It also has the setup: when the lines were drawn, why, and how many upward and downward lines stood then (§2 draws them all). The first N rows of each table are picked; tick or untick rows to pick others. The tables can be sorted, searched and downloaded.

2 · The picked trades, two charts each

Every trade picked in §1, long trades first, in the tables' order, with two charts.
  • The big picture (top). Daily candles from some sessions before the entry (the slider), with every line that stood when the trade was set up. Each line comes from one chart of the top-down walk, from the monthly down to the 15-minute chart, and is drawn in that chart's style: monthly, weekly and daily lines solid, 4-hour dashed, 1-hour dash-dotted, 15-minute dotted. The higher the chart, the heavier the line. The line the trade bounced off is bold, and the window of the detailed chart is shaded.
  • The detail (below). The 15-minute candles from the point A of the line the trade bounced off, or from a few sessions before the entry if that is earlier, to a few sessions after the exit. It shows the same lines, and the candles that fixed the traded line: ◆ point A, ★ the candle that stopped the ray, ◇ point B. When the traded line starts before the stock's 15-minute history, the note under the trade says so; its point A is then on the big picture only. Also: the entry gap, the moment the lines were drawn (dotted), the entry, the stop at every close, the exit and the trade (shaded). Zoom in with the mouse; double-click to zoom back out.
Upward lines are blue, downward lines orange. Hover over a line or an anchor for its details; the table under each trade lists its lines. Part 2 · When does it pay? Profitable time ranges

The question behind this part: can something we can measure tell, better than luck, that a stock is moving into a stretch where the bounce pays? A side's record is its return after costs, compounded trade by trade. A zigzag cuts the record into legs: a rising leg ends once the record falls by the reversal from its high, a falling leg once it rises by the reversal from its low. A rising leg of at least min trades trades is a profitable range, from its first trade's entry to its last trade's exit. A range is known only after it ends: the ranges are the target of the question, and a metric meant to predict them must be read before a range starts. Both sliders apply at once, without replaying.

4 · Every leg of each record

Every leg the zigzag found, profitable or not: the profitable ranges are the target, the losing legs the contrast the next step needs. return is the leg's own return after costs (%), stock move the stock's from the leg's first entry to its last exit (%), best trade's share the part of a rising leg's gain that came from its best trade (near 1: one trade made the range). The table can be sorted, filtered and downloaded.

6 · Do the wins cluster more than luck would make them?

A range is no evidence by itself: any record of wins and losses has rising legs. The test keeps every trade's size and time and deals the record's wins and losses out again at random, 2,000 times (the same number of wins each time). It reads persistence directly: the correlation of a trade's return with the next one's, with the average of the five before it, and the number of streaks of wins or losses (fewer streaks = more clustered). chance by luck is the share of random deals at least as clustered as the real record. The zigzag's own numbers would make a poor test: ten wins in a row then ten losses spend no more trades in profitable ranges than 40% of the random deals do. long (129 trades): more clustered than luck on streaks of wins or losses.
short (120 trades): no sign of clustering: every statistic lies where random deals of the same trades put it. With a few dozen trades a side, only strong clustering can show here. If none shows, the record gives no hint that stretches exist. A market metric could still sort the trades, so the next step tests candidate metrics directly against the legs.
